title: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming; and this holds good.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera”. Scope: genera of plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Current divergence can proxy species formation in well-sampled clades, but no global dataset consistently identifies incipient species. Available data test restricted groups and depend on contested speciation metrics.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate current incipient-speciation rates from genomic divergence, reproductive isolation and lineage splitting, then test whether they increase with existing genus richness after age and sampling controls. A positive average relationship supports the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genus age and taxonomic practice strongly confound richness.

'Still forming' is not directly observable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.61
discriminating power: 0.5
data existence: 0.78
data adequacy: 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Dated trees make a richness-versus-recent-speciation regression possible for vertebrates and some plants. The prediction is close to a measurable variable, but rate artifacts and uneven species sampling are large. The test is a real one for well-sampled clades and a proxy for genera of plants and animals in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare recent speciation rates, or counts of subspecies and phylogeographic splits, with present genus richness. A positive average relationship would support the prediction that where many species have formed, many are still forming; no relationship, or a negative one, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Subspecies counts repeat the effort bias that affects variety counts.

A large genus can be old and slow, which satisfies 'many have formed' without 'many are still forming'.

Tip-rate estimators are biased by tree shape, sampling fraction, and taxonomic splitting.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.76
operationalizability: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.46
analysis feasibility: 0.64
